chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Hilal, from Uqbah ibn Khalid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Regarding

A man purchased goods from another, and made the purchase binding, but he left the goods with the seller and did not take possession of them, and said, 'I will come to you tomorrow, if God wills.' The goods were then stolen. Whose money would they be? He (peace be upon him) said: 'From the money of the owner of the goods who is in his house, until he takes possession of the goods and removes them from his house. When he removes them from his house, the buyer is liable for their value until he returns their money to him.'
ai.seo_question: Who bears the risk of loss if goods are stolen before being taken possession of in an Islamic sale?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the principle of *qabd* (possession) as the decisive factor for transferring risk (*daman*) in sales, a cornerstone of Shia fiqh regarding conditional sales. It distinguishes between mere agreement and physical transfer, establishing that liability shifts to the buyer only upon actual removal of the goods from the seller's domain, reflecting the practical legal standards of early Islamic commerce.
